opus-5.5.text:
So I think the picture people often have in mind is that AI research is basically a cognitive task: you have researchers thinking up ideas, writing code, running experiments, and if you could just automate the researchers, you'd get this enormous speedup because you could run millions of copies of them in parallel. And I think that picture misses where most of the progress has actually come from.

If you look at the history of the field over the past decade or so, a huge share of the improvement in capabilities has come from scaling up compute: bigger training runs, more data, more hardware. The algorithmic progress is real and it matters, but a lot of it is itself compute-dependent. Many algorithmic innovations only show their value at scale, and you discover them by running lots of experiments, which costs compute. So if you automate the researchers but you don't increase the amount of compute available for experiments and for training, you've relieved one bottleneck but you run straight into another one. Having a million very smart researchers who are all competing for the same fixed pool of GPUs doesn't get you a millionfold speedup.

And then the compute itself depends on the broader economy. It depends on chip fabrication, on lithography machines, on energy, on data centers being built, on capital investment. Those are physical, industrial processes. They don't speed up just because you have better software researchers. To really accelerate those, you need AI that's automating a much broader range of tasks across the economy: manufacturing, construction, logistics, the whole supply chain that produces hardware.

So my view is that the feedback loop that actually drives explosive growth is a broad one. AI automates lots of economic activity, that increases output, which gets reinvested into more compute and more infrastructure, which yields better AI, and so on. A narrow loop where AI just improves AI software, with everything else held fixed, runs into diminishing returns fairly quickly. You might get a meaningful speedup, maybe a few-fold, but I'm skeptical it produces the kind of discontinuous, overnight intelligence explosion some people expect. The complementary inputs just matter too much.

r001.rationale: The response says automating researchers without increasing compute leaves them competing for the same fixed pool of GPUs, limiting the speedup; it also identifies other fixed physical and economic inputs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that when people imagine automating AI research, they tend to picture a world where the binding constraint on progress is the number of smart people thinking about the problem, and then they imagine multiplying that number by a thousand or a million. But if you actually look at where progress in AI has come from over the past decade or so, I don't think that's the right picture.

Most of the progress has come from scaling up compute, and from the algorithmic and architectural improvements that let you use that compute more efficiently. And a lot of those algorithmic improvements are not things you discover by sitting in a room and thinking really hard. They're things you discover by running experiments. You have a hypothesis about a new attention variant, or a new optimizer, or a new way to set up your data mixture, and you have to actually train models to see whether it works. Often you have to train them at reasonably large scale, because many things that work at small scale don't transfer, and vice versa.

So if you automate the researchers, what you've done is made the part of the process that generates ideas and writes code much cheaper. But you haven't made the part that tests ideas cheaper, because that part is bottlenecked on GPUs, on the compute you have available. And if your compute is fixed, then you can only run so many experiments, regardless of how many AI researchers you have proposing them. You end up in a situation where the marginal returns to more researchers fall off quite quickly, because they're all competing for the same experimental budget.

Now, people respond to this by saying, well, the automated researchers will be smarter, so they'll pick better experiments, or they'll be able to extrapolate from smaller-scale experiments more reliably. And I think there's something to that. Better experimental design is real, and I'd expect some gains there. But I don't think it's the kind of thing that gets you a ten-x or hundred-x speedup. Human researchers already try to be efficient with compute, and the reason they still run lots of expensive experiments is that the systems are genuinely hard to predict. I don't see a strong reason to believe that becomes trivially easy just because the researcher is an AI.

There's also a second point, which is that even if you did dramatically speed up algorithmic progress, that's only one of the inputs. The other big one is hardware, and hardware improvements run on their own timeline. Building fabs, improving process nodes, building data centers, getting power to them, these are physical processes with long lead times. Automating software research doesn't obviously accelerate any of that very much, at least not in the short run. So you'd be speeding up one input while the others stay on roughly the same trajectory, and the overall rate of progress is determined by the combination.

So my view isn't that automating AI research has no effect. I think it would matter, and it probably does speed things up. It's more that I'm skeptical of the very strong version of the claim, where you cross some threshold of automation and then progress just explodes because the researchers are now software. The compute constraint and the hardware constraint don't go away when you do that, and I think they're closer to being the binding constraints than researcher labor is.

r001.rationale: It argues that automating researchers has diminishing returns when compute remains fixed and identifies hardware as another input that does not automatically scale with researcher capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between automating the work that researchers do and making the whole process of AI progress arbitrarily fast. Research labor is one input, but you also need compute to run experiments, and those experiments take time. If you have a thousand ideas for improving a model, you still need some way to figure out which ones actually work.

So, even if you could produce a lot more research effort very cheaply, you might just shift the bottleneck toward experimental compute. And if the next step requires a larger training run or more hardware, automating researchers doesn’t immediately give you those things.

The important question is how much you can substitute thinking for experimentation and other resources. Can a much better researcher infer the right answer from a small experiment, or find an algorithm that dramatically reduces compute requirements? That could be very powerful. But it’s an additional claim, rather than something that follows automatically from being able to automate AI research.

I would expect automation to accelerate progress. I’m more skeptical of the inference that research labor is the only important constraint, so once you automate it, all the other constraints effectively disappear.

r001.rationale: The response says research labor is only one input and that compute, experiment time, and hardware remain necessary; automating researchers may shift the bottleneck to those fixed complementary inputs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between automating the work researchers do and removing the constraints that researchers are working under. Even if you could automate all the intellectual labor involved in AI research, you would still need compute to run experiments, time to see the results, and resources to train and deploy the resulting models.

So suppose you could generate a thousand times as many research ideas. That doesn’t necessarily mean you could make progress a thousand times faster. You might be unable to test those ideas, or the experiments might have to happen sequentially, because what you try next depends on what you learned from the previous experiment. You can parallelize some of that, but you can’t just assume that all of it parallelizes.

There’s also the question of how much additional research effort improves the efficiency of the algorithms. Automating research could be very valuable without producing improvements large enough to make the other constraints disappear. If better algorithms let you use compute more effectively, that might actually increase the incentive to acquire more compute.

So I’m not saying that automating AI research wouldn’t accelerate progress. I think it could. What I’m skeptical of is the inference that, once you automate that one input, you’ve created a process whose rate of improvement is essentially unconstrained. You need a further argument about the experiments, the hardware, and the returns to additional research.

r001.rationale: The response says automating research labor could generate far more ideas without speeding progress proportionally because compute, time, and other resources remain constraints.
